newsitem.title: UK: UK/Sinn Fein contacts no surprise, loyalists say.
newsitem.headline: UK/Sinn Fein contacts no surprise, loyalists say.

text.p: Northern Ireland loyalist politicians said on Tuesday that British government contacts with the political wing of the IRA were no surprise and would not derail the fragile peace process.
"These contacts with Sinn Fein are to be expected unfortunately," said David Ervine, leader of the Progressive Unionist Party, after talks with British Prime Minister Tony Blair.
But he added that it would have been better for the government to honour its promises.
Blair said a month ago he was severing official contacts with Sinn Fein because of the deaths of two policemen in an Irish Republican Army (IRA) ambush.

But Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam on Monday acknowledged that officials had been in touch with Sinn Fein after the group sought clarification of the requirements for its admission to peace talks.
"I'm not particularly dismayed, I don't think it matters a damn," Ervine said.

And in a reference to previous comments from Blair that the peace process "train" would leave on time with or without the IRA, Ervine said: "I am convinced the station master certainly seems determined to take the train out on time." He forecast full talks would start in September.

With Ervine was Gary McMichael, leader of the Ulster Democratic Party. Both his and Ervine's parties have close links with Protestant paramilitary groups and want Northern Ireland to remain part of Britain.
After what he described as an "extremely frank" meeting with the British Prime Minister, McMichael said it was time for the IRA to make its mind up.
"Either they are prepared to engage in the process...or they are not. If they are not, the process moves forward without them."

A government spokesman said Blair had praised the Loyalist's measured response and urged them to continue with it. He said the peace process would continue with or without the IRA, although he wanted them on board.
